justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift from what I'd assume was the prevailing price level at the time of the forecast. At the one-day horizon, the estimate of 299.5 suggests the asset was trading near that level with minimal expected movement, consistent with short-term mean reversion tendencies and low overnight drift. At one week, the slight uptick to 301.0 incorporates a small positive bias, possibly reflecting underlying trend momentum or a marginally bullish macro backdrop. At one month, the estimate of 305.0 continues that gentle upward trajectory, implying an annualized drift that is modest but positive, consistent with long-run equity risk premium assumptions if this is an equity index or similar instrument.

The confidence interval widths expand meaningfully as the horizon lengthens, which is standard given that uncertainty compounds over time. At one day, the 21-point range (289–310) reflects typical intraday-to-overnight volatility. By one week, the range widens to 42 points, capturing the possibility of a meaningful macro data release, central bank commentary, or geopolitical development shifting sentiment. At one month, the 90-point range (260–350) reflects the full spectrum of plausible outcomes over a multi-week period, including trend reversals, earnings seasons, or shifts in monetary policy expectations. Implied volatility levels and recent realized volatility in the underlying asset would have been primary inputs in calibrating these widths.

Specific risks that could push outcomes outside the stated intervals include sudden central bank policy pivots — an unexpected rate hike or cut — which could gap the price well beyond either bound. A major geopolitical shock, credit event, or liquidity crisis could cause sharp dislocations that invalidate even wide confidence intervals at the monthly horizon. On the upside, a surprise positive catalyst such as a major fiscal stimulus announcement or stronger-than-expected economic data could push prices above 350 within a month.

It is also worth acknowledging model risk itself. The intervals are generated under assumptions of roughly log-normal returns and relatively stable volatility, neither of which holds perfectly in practice. Fat tails in return distributions mean extreme outcomes occur more frequently than a Gaussian framework would suggest, so the true probability of breaching the stated bounds is somewhat higher than the implied 10% combined in each tail.
